items.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
items.excerpt: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday. Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: Read full article Comments

items.title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
items.excerpt: As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips. Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even pre-order a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit. Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950 . It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars got to go for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer , but we haven't had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate. items.title: Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos
items.excerpt: Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System. The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan's flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan's heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. items.title: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn't seen for decades
items.excerpt: Pennsylvania's health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn't been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory. The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania. As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though the latest reported death is still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally). items.title: Russian spacecraft maneuvers in "extreme proximity" to satellite used by Ukraine
items.excerpt: A Russian military satellite maneuvered in "extreme proximity" of a commercial Earth-imaging satellite in recent days in the first known example an unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit, according to the orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. The Russian spacecraft, Kosmos 2612, "conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36, a US-operated commercial imaging satellite," LeoLabs said. "Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to extreme proximity to ICEYE-X36. It then maneuvered around ICEYE-X36, remained nearby for an extended period, and then began moving away." US military officials and independent analysts have tracked Kosmos 2612 since its April launch on a Soyuz rocket from a spaceport in northern Russia. Within weeks, it became apparent that at least four of the six satellites from that launch were stalking ICEYE-X36 after they adjusted orbits to line up with the orbit of the ICEYE spacecraft. items.title: openclaw / openclaw
items.excerpt: # OpenClaw 🦞 — Your assistant, on your devices, in your chats OpenClaw is an open-source AI assistant that runs on your own computer and meets you in the channels you already use: Discord, iMessage, Slack, Teams, Telegram, WhatsApp, and 20+ more, plus native apps for macOS, iOS, Android, Windows, and Linux. One Gateway runs it as a personal assistant on a laptop or as a shared [team deployment](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/teams); configuration is the only difference. **Yours, with no catch.** State, memory, and credentials live on your hardware. Models and agent harnesses (Claude, Codex, local models) are plugins you can swap without changing anything else. Your prompts go to the model provider and chat platforms you configure, plus any diagnostics export you enable yourself; by default OpenClaw itself phones home for nothing but a daily version check, anonymous feature statistics are opt-in, and `update.checkOnStart: false` disables both ([what OpenClaw sends](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/telemetry)). OpenClaw is stewarded by the [OpenClaw Foundation](https://openclaw.org), an independent 501(c)(3), and has no paid tier, hosted service, or token. The architecture case — trusted gateway, untrusted execution, policy enforced by code — is in [Why OpenClaw](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/why-openclaw). items.title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
items.excerpt: Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep. items.title: How to Know When an AI Agent Can Work Unsupervised — Evan Kormos, Coinbase
items.excerpt: Evan Kormos, a player-coach at Coinbase with 15 years in enterprise financial services, lays out a practical way to bring agents into policy-driven, regulated workflows. He models processes as DAGs and loops, explains why a loop is only as trustworthy as its check, and shows how evals and traces become a new confidence mechanism. Agents then move through three stages: fully supervised, then sampled, then humans handling only exceptions. items.title: Smarter Models Killed the Harness. Here's What's Left — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI
items.excerpt: Is the agent harness dead? Jediah Katz, Cursor's longest-tenured agent-harness engineer and now at SpaceX, explains why fancy harnesses no longer add coding intelligence: the data flywheel teaches models the skills harnesses used to patch in. He then argues why the harness matters more than ever. It opens new frontiers like Grokbot, and it owns what models can't absorb: infrastructure, trust and security, and efficiency. He closes with predictions, including that 90% of agent work runs off the laptop within six months. items.excerpt: Quickstart · Headroom for Teams · Install · Proof · Agents · Docs · Discord · llms.txt AI agents / LLMs: read /llms.txt here, or fetch the live index · full docs blob . Headroom compresses everything your AI agent reads — tool outputs, logs, RAG chunks, files, and conversation history — before it reaches the LLM. Same answers, fraction of the tokens. Compression runs on your machine; no prompt or file content is sent anywhere to be compressed. 10,144 → 1,260 tokens. The same FATAL found. ## What it does - **Library** — `compress(messages)` in Python or TypeScript, inline in any app. - **Proxy** — `headroom proxy --port 8787`, zero code changes, any language. - **Agent wrap** — `headroom wrap claude|codex|grok|copilot|cursor|aider|opencode|cline|continue|goose|openhands|openclaw|vibe|omp|zcode` in one command; undo with `headroom unwrap `. - **MCP server** — `headroom_compress`, `headroom_retrieve`, `headroom_stats` for any MCP client. - **Cross-agent memory** — one shared store across Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok, with automatic dedup. - **`headroom learn`** — mines failed sessions and writes corrections to `CLAUDE.local.md` (default, gitignored), `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md` or `GROK.md`. - **Output token reduction** — trims what the model *writes back*, not only what you send. items.title: 1000 Years of AI Safety
items.excerpt: A three-year AI pause could buy 1000 years' worth of AI safety work. See: https://1000yearsofaisafety.com How much AI safety work a pause produces, in years of the whole 2025 AI safety field's work . The government bans new large training runs and gets the top three US labs to redirect their GPUs and researchers to safety research. We developed a model of an AI pause that estimates how much AI safety research it produces. We don't know what the pause will look like, so we modeled five durations, four AI capability levels and four levels of trust in AI. We’ll use it to improve Plan A, but it already shows a few things: A three-year pause produces 1000x more AI safety research than was done in 2025. A nine-year pause produces 100,000x more. Checking it all takes an army. If you let AI work autonomously for 9 years, you will need 2.8 million verifiers to check it all. With safer verification protocols, it goes down to 150k verifiers. Without an army, you still get a lot. In the worst case, you still get 44% of the potential AI safety research. That's because not all research is equally important, and the labs' own staff verify the most important research first. Even AI 2040's strict Plan A produces a lot of AI safety research. In Plan A, external auditors approve every line of code before it runs. This cuts total AI safety work to 3–7% of the potential, but it's still 1000x more than in 2025. items.title: A Tourist Mathematician’s Apologia: Living in a Human-AGI World
items.excerpt: Graham Greene described G. H. Hardy’s 1940 book, A Mathematician’s Apology , as the best account of what it is like to be a creative artist. Hardy had many friends, wide-ranging interests that included the game of cricket, and empathy for the less well-off. But it was his creative work in pure mathematics that gave Hardy “the one great permanent happiness of my life.” “Mathematics,” writes C. P. Snow, “was his [Hardy’s] justification.” It gave meaning to his life. Fast forward to October 2026, when OpenAI released more than 700 AI-generated documents claiming to have solved or made major progress in over 300 areas of mathematics. Many of these are ‘solutions’ to the most difficult mathematical concepts that have challenged mathematicians for decades and some for centuries. Mathematicians used to spend entire lifetimes, as Hardy did, solving only one or a few of these problems. OpenAI deployed an advanced ‘reasoning’ LLM and a swarm of 10,000 AI agents that required an average of only three hours of computation per solution. The solutions to these 700-plus problems were ‘checked’ not by humans but by another computer program, making the process almost entirely free of human intervention. What has remained human is the posing of the question, the way it is framed and input into the AI, and of course the design and then training of the AI. Will these too soon be done by AI? How would Hardy have reacted? What would he have said? What advice might he give us as AIs take over more…

But in 2022 I did an interpretability project on a Go-playing model and have spent quite some time thinking about Go-playing AIs. Why I found this surprising Go is the canonical domain where AI models are considered to be vastly, vastly superhuman. We heard it from the best Go players themselves, who have faced off and been defeated by these Go-playing AIs. Ke Jie, the professional Go player then ranked world No. 1, said in 2017 after losing to AlphaGo that “AlphaGo to me is 100 percent perfection, to me AlphaGo is the god of the Go game”. I've been interested in Go-playing AIs partly because it serves as an intuition pump for me for superintelligence in other domains: Just imagine if an AI model became as superhuman in software/math/business strategy/persuasion as Go models in fact are. items.title: GLM-5.1 Has ~Astra Level CoT Control
items.excerpt: TL;DR. We run the CoT-Control evaluation suite on GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek models and find that while Kimi and DeepSeek models have poor CoT control, GLM models are outliers in their ability to control CoT. We extensively investigate this behavior in GLM-5.1 and show that previous generation GLM models (GLM-4.5 and GLM-4.7) also have similarly high levels of CoT control. We also find that despite its high controllability, GLM-5.1 performs poorly at monitor evasion tasks. However, a model that can control its CoT can potentially evade a monitor by suppressing relevant information, adding irrelevant information or modifying how the information is presented. Indeed, GPT-6-Astra has high CoT controllability and is effective at evading monitors when instructed. System card . This blogpost investigates CoT controllability in leading open-source models. items.title: What do the other 80 percent mean?
items.excerpt: I am Austrian and wrote this in German. The English is a literal machine translation, not rewritten. Everywhere now, catastrophic harm to humanity is being discussed, and various scenarios. But the other percentages are not mapped in detail by outcome, the way it is done with nuclear scenarios, where people look at this more closely. That is possible. People do not go deeper, they do not use this method. When I heard it for the first time, I did not trust my ears. I thought this was fake news. Unfortunately not. If 25 percent means the extinction of humanity, does 75 percent mean paradise? Whoever names twenty percent extinction does not claim to have the rest under control. That is a deception, a false assumption. It could mean that most people die and only a few survive. Or that most people suffer. That is not clear. Or does it mean the collapse of our systems, the overload of our society, chaos and unrest, total concentration of power and control? Or pure happiness and sunshine? In the interviews nobody asks about it. No reporter, no senate, no government. What is actually connected? Production systems, communication systems, payment systems, navigation systems. Also facilities operated under hazard supervision, nuclear, chemical, biological. In principle, the digital world is the habitat of silicon intelligence. So the twice a year Times & Places posts are a helpful chance to check for signs of life and get an update on the local meetup communities. But the most important part is coordination. If you only go to one ACX meetup a year, we suggest you go to the fall ACX Everywhere in your city. That way if there was secretly a dozen of you all making the assumption that you were the only reader in the area, you could all show up at the fall meetup and realize the conspiracy was larger than you thought. And in fact many local ACX groups got their start by just such a rallying flag. A few were even started by a traveling reader who volunteered to run a meetup in a city they didn’t live in, but locals showed up, took the banner, and kept the meetup going. This year we have meetups planned in over a hundred and eighty cities, from Aachen, Germany to Zagreb, Croatia. items.title: AI Safety Is Not A Corporate Plot
items.excerpt: AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have long mentioned the possibility that their products could be existentially dangerous, but this has recently crescendoed into even more dire warnings, including suggestions that we have to pace the frontier , ie coordinate to slow AI progress. In response, cynical commentators have suggested this is a conspiracy to boost the companies’ stocks. The exact motives imputed vary from person to person. Some say the companies are hyping the product by talking about how dangerous it is; if AI is smart enough to kill all humans, it must be smart enough for your business workflow. Others say they’re trying to distract from near-term harms; every inch of newspaper space devoted to human extinction is one less inch that can be spent on plagiarism and water use. But the most popular story involves regulatory capture: if the product is unsafe, maybe it can only be trusted to a few big politically-connected companies, and everyone else should be banned. Many debates about AI are complicated and hard to resolve, but this one isn’t: all of these stories are clearly false. Some evidence: The AI experts who aren’t affiliated with big companies are just as concerned as the ones who are. The AI company leaders giving these warnings were giving the exact same warnings before they had AI companies - and in many cases, before they worked in the industry, or before the industry existed. If these corporate plots were real, they would be incredibly dumb.…

items.title: The China Price
items.excerpt: In 1971, as the international monetary system was on the brink of collapse, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Connally told a group of worried European finance ministers that the dollar was “our currency, but your problem.” The dollar had become that system’s official reserve currency in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreement, making signatories subject to the whims of U.S. monetary policy. Even after Bretton Woods collapsed and many currencies floated freely, the dollar continued to dominate. In the last half century, U.S. currency power has only expanded, as more countries have integrated into the global economy and therefore grown to depend on the dollar. China, reliant on export-driven growth, is foremost among them.

items.title: Is Netanyahu’s Grip on Israel Slipping?
items.excerpt: Israel votes soon in an election shaped by the Oct. 7 attacks and the war in Gaza that followed. With former general Gadi Eisenkot’s party holding a slight lead in the polls, could this be the end of Benjamin Netanyahu’s long reign as prime minister? An Eisenkot victory, however, is unlikely to signal a major shift in foreign policy, reflecting a broader rightward turn in Israeli politics. Beyond domestic policy, the outcome of the election carries significant regional stakes and could reshape Israel’s ties with other countries, including the US. items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: This Peptide Could Repair Early Tooth Decay WITHOUT Drilling! 🦷
items.excerpt: 🦷 **PEPTIDE REPAIRS TEETH?!** Scientists are studying a remarkable peptide called **P11-4** that could change how dentists treat early tooth decay! What if we could stop some cavities before drilling or fillings become necessary? 🔬 **Meet P11-4 — a self-assembling peptide with exciting potential in dental medicine.** When tooth enamel begins losing minerals, P11-4 can enter early damaged areas and form a microscopic scaffold that supports remineralization. items.title: CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?
items.excerpt: Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. items.title: GardenBench: A lightweight, daily evaluation of LLM capabilities
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce GardenBench, a benchmark with 11 test suites that evaluate the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a range of tasks. By systematically prompting LLMs with various lightweight queries, we document day-to-day changes in model performance, including run costs and times, that other benchmarks miss. This allows us to compare the accuracy and features of responses across model providers and versions. We account for daily variations in model accuracy, capturing both model progress and degradation, for instance, when a model is changed post-deployment or when a new model is released. We base our evaluation on general-use tasks and make our results publicly accessible via a live dashboard, diversifying existing approaches to LLM testing. Our main contribution is an innovative, lightweight, and inexpensive benchmark, designed to be consumer-facing and for everyday tasks.

items.title: Doing Less with More: A First-Principles Exploration of the Suitability of Agentic Computing over Alternative Architectural Choices
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is growing interest in automating business activities with Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) due to latter's seeming ease of use. Never has it been easier, or costlier, to do less with more. However, little is known about when agents are preferable to established alternatives such as local computation, Representational State Transfer (REST), the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), particularly when development speed, performance, and operational cost are considered. We investigate this question using a controlled mathematical task that compares seven methods on a benchmark of 1,000 arithmetic expressions where semantics of operator precedence has to be preserved. We ran this setup across a native Function Calling baseline (Python library), REST, SOAP and MCP microservice architectures, direct responses from large language models (LLMs) using a Groq cloud API and five locally deployed Ollama models, and agentic systems in which five local LLMs invoke MCP tools. The deterministic methods achieve 100% accuracy with negligible latency. Direct LLM evaluation achieves at most 92.9% accuracy at over 22,000x the latency of a native function call. With MCP tools, the best agent reaches 99.9% accuracy, but incurs nearly 1,000,000x the baseline latency. These results demonstrate that LLMs approaches are poorly suited for exact arithmetic evaluation and motivate an informed architectural…

items.title: A Controlled LLM Workflow for Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis of Risk Score Differences
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.23962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a controlled Large Language Model (LLM) workflow for explaining risk score differences using similar historical transactions. The workflow combines reference retrieval and contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) evidence with reference-based LLM reasoning and deterministic validation. Experiments on a test dataset show that the workflow produces more consistent, evidence-grounded and traceable diagnoses than the same LLM without structured workflow guidance.

items.title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies…

items.title: Beyond Explicit Intent: Discovering and Shaping Artistic Intent through Human-AI Co-Creation
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI is becoming an important medium for artistic creation, yet existing interactions often assume that creators can specify intentions in advance and accurately communicate them through text prompts. Artistic intentions, however, may be vague, latent, or recognizable only after seeing concrete visual possibilities. We propose a human-AI co-creation paradigm beyond explicit intent expression. By expanding model exploration, we expose artists to diverse visual possibilities, allowing them to identify previously unarticulated preferences through observation, comparison, and selection. We then integrate artists' curatorial judgments into reinforcement learning, assigning different learning strengths based on preferences over generation trajectories, so recognized directions are more strongly reinforced and the model gradually adapts to individual aesthetics. This creates a continuous "explore-identify-shape-re-explore" loop in which artistic intent is progressively discovered, externalized, and shaped. Through three user studies, we examine latent-preference discovery, personalized preference alignment, and the externalization of vague, difficult-to-express creative intentions.

items.title: The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
items.excerpt: For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine. AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls. We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different. AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. items.title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org
items.excerpt: Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose. To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer. We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen , a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization. Meet Evergreen Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows: Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo’s outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed. Stale repository detection and archival. Repos with no human activity past a threshold get flagged, warned, and (if still untouched) archived. Two design principles shaped everything: Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. The safe outcome is the default outcome. Never destroy anything. Evergreen will never delete a repository or its contents. Archived repos are recoverable, and every access change is written…

items.excerpt: Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months. The short version of August and September : we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete. By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added. We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. items.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers
items.excerpt: Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away. Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page. The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people. But returning less data didn’t actually make the query any cheaper. Now maintainers have a direct way to get the curve: we built an endpoint that returns up to 30 weeks of daily star counts in a single request, with no identities attached. Keeping that cheap to serve meant reducing how much data the database processed, not just how much it returned, and the endpoint does that by filtering stars by time before it counts anything . What maintainers need from star history We first addressed the immediate risks to developers and to our database by restricting stargazer and watcher lists to repository administrators and collaborators . items.title: Drug company gifts, meals, and payments to doctors lead to worse prescribing, review of 93 studies finds
items.excerpt: Key findings Pharmaceutical marketing aimed at doctors, from gifts to meals and payments, may increase inappropriate prescribing and the quantity and cost of prescriptions. Conflict‐of‐interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between pharmaceutical companies and doctors can limit prescribing of inappropriate drugs and overprescribing. Gifts, payments, free meals, and other marketing ploys by pharmaceutical companies heavily influence doctors to prescribe more drugs, choose less appropriate treatments, and drive up prescription costs, according to a systematic review of 93 studies. These prescribing choices can expose patients to drugs that offer fewer benefits, cause more side effects or are unnecessary, while increasing health system costs. The review , published today [October 9] in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, found that policies restricting interactions between drug companies and doctors were associated with better prescribing choices, lower costs, and possibly fewer prescriptions. “Overall, when doctors have more contact with drug company promotion, prescribing tends to become less appropriate, more frequent, and more expensive,” said co-author Dr. Lisa Bero, an affiliate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Center of Bioethics and Humanities. “This is problematic for a number of reasons, and it matters because it directly affects patient care.” Dr. Quinn Grundy, director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for…

items.title: Hormone-disrupting chemical mixtures linked to excess childhood weight
items.excerpt: Key findings Multiple hormone-disrupting chemicals were linked to obesity from childhood through adolescence. Prenatal exposure to metals, organochlorine pesticides, and PFAS was linked to higher obesity. Childhood exposure to phenols and certain phthalates was linked to more body fat in adolescence. Children exposed during pregnancy and early life to combinations of chemicals that disrupt hormones and metabolism may face a greater risk of excess weight that persists into adolescence, a new study suggests. Published this month [September 2026] in Environment International , the study followed 1,301 mother-child pairs from six European birth cohorts. Researchers measured prenatal and childhood exposure to 45 endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) across nine chemical classes. These included per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS), phthalates , pesticides , polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBs), flame retardants, metals, parabens, and phenols, including bisphenol A (BPA) and triclosan. Researchers found that greater exposure to certain combinations of EDCs was associated with higher BMI. They also found links to more body fat and higher odds of overweight. About 28% of the children had overweight or obesity at age 8, rising to about 30% by age 15. The findings add to growing evidence linking chemical exposures during critical stages of development to obesity risk.
